editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of a taped interview with Bernard C. Digman, conducted by Tom Swope on July 22, 2001, on behalf of the Veterans Oral History Project. The interview took place in Willoughby Hills, Ohio, and is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Bernard Clare (ph) Digman. Bernie served in the U.S. Navy. He served in the Pacific Theatre, and his highest rank was Lieutenant (JG). I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Digman's home in Willoughby Hills, Ohio, on July 22, 2001. Bernie was 78 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Question: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: Answer: 1943. I was in for about three years, and I got out in 1946.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Were you drafted, or did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Oh, no. I am glad to tell you that I enlisted. I did not get drafted. Do you want some details on my training and so forth?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Sure, sure.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Because I have --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: I think you went into the Navy, right?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yeah, I went into the Navy. In fact, my home is in East Liverpool, Ohio, and I went to Steubenville, Ohio, where you enlist in the Air Force and in the Army, which is what I went to do. So I went down with a friend, and while I was waiting for him in the hallway, a man handed me a picture of the test that you take for color blindness, and he said, "Can you read this?" And I said "Sure, I can read this." I read it and then he handed me something else, and by the time I went home that evening, I was in the Navy... 'cause I never did like water {laughs}, but I lived with it. I trained in several places, in Walla Walla, California and Livermore, California and Corpus Christi, Texas, which was where I got my wings. I was -- I chose to fly multi-engine airplanes 'cause there was one airplane I liked especially, called the A20, so I looked forward to doing that, and as you might guess, the service does just whatever you don't want to do, and I ended up in one that I wanted to stay away from, which was a TBF, the biggest one the Navy had, as a matter of fact, a single engine. Ended up in that one. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: That's a torpedo bomber, right?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: That is a torpedo bomber. Most of my Navy experience in flying was in Air-Sea Rescue, and I'll get into some of that just a little bit later. I trained in Jacksonville, Florida. I went through twin-engine Beechcraft, and went to Jacksonville, Florida, trained in a PBY, and from there I was sent to Pearl Harbor to do shore patrol duty, which is what I did most of the time. And I was in a squadron there for awhile, and then they sent me to Hawaii, which was to an airfield in the city named Kaneohe. And there we had a squadron of PBYs and PB2Ys, and I spent a lot of time there in the air patrol and so forth. It was like a job with me. We would go out every morning on patrol. They would give us a big map before we went to tell us the directions and so forth. The map would have vectors on it which would be just like a road map, and you'd -- it always had three vectors, and you would fly in a big triangle and then come back home. Each one of those vectors were, oh, three-to-four hours long, so that made your trip maybe 12 hours a day which is a pretty long day, and it's a lot of gasoline. And when you hear the word "Navy," you think of water, and boy, I saw a lot of water. And I kind of enjoyed it; it wasn't too hazardous but we -- the war was still going on over in the South Pacific and we did some interesting thing and no real hazardous things, and we were out there to record and report whatever we saw and whatever we did. And the -- I remember we'd seen several submarines; we carried a bomb one time and dropped it; I don't know if we hit the submarine or if we didn't hit the submarine. And one day a couple of Zeros did some barrel rolls around us, but we really had no armor, and why they did that and left, I don't ever know and I don't care, now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: But they didn't shoot at you.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: But they didn't shoot at us, yeah. And we used to use JDOH to take off with -- those are rockets that you put on the side of a big PB2Y -- so anyhow, I had a lot of experience in that PB2Y, and one day, after a few weeks, there was a little guy from Washington D.C. come over, and he made all of our PB2Ys obsolete. Those were called Coronados, and they're four-engine. The PBY that I talked about in Jacksonville is only two-engines. So they said you're -- me and six of my buddies -- they said, "You're out of PB2Ys and you're going to fly TBFs now. Well, we didn't much like that idea because we were multi-engine pilots and that's what we wanted to fly, but you don't have much say, really, in the Navy. It's probably the same with the Air Force. So they switched us over, and the transition there had to be with an AT6, which is an SN3 in the Navy, and we had to fly that, as I say, the transition between multi-engine and single engine. But we made it through, we soloed and so forth. You want me to keep going?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Why'd you prefer the multi-engine over the single engine?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, the airplane that I saw that I liked back before I knew too much about airplanes was an A20, which is a medium bomber. Beautiful airplane. In fact, we had one here in Cleveland for quite a while. That's what I wanted to fly, and I pointed all my efforts to get into that to fly it, and it never happened -- I think I got inside one once -- it was a big disappointment to me. So I went to single engine; well, I had to 'cause they made me do that. But in a TBF which is a huge, big airplane, when you check out in it you don't have an instructor because there's only one seat in it. And I remember my friends, my buddies -- my other buddies were watching each of us fly and get kind of checked out it in. And the first time I went up in this big airplane by myself, there were three sailors that wanted to take a ride with me, 'cause they could get in the back end. And I said, "I've never flown the airplane before," and it seemed not to bother them. But it bothered me more than it did them. So they climbed in the back and enjoyed the ride and thanked me, and it was just that easy. So {chuckling} that's why I was -- how I checked out in the TBF. The reason for the TBFs was that they have bomb bay for torpedoes, which we didn't have, but we had life rafts. And it worked out very nicely, because we were more -- we could get out quicker, get back quicker, we could carry what we needed, and that was the kind of duty that was. And our group, or our Air-Sea Rescue part of the Navy was maybe the only group that, we should have been called "Boy, are we glad to see you!" group, if you know what I mean.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: What was the unit number and --

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: What was it? What was your -- your squadron? What was the unit?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: The designation; what squadron was it?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: I don't even remember a designation. It was in Hawaii, and we were at Kaneohe, and as I told you, we did Patrol Duty. But they changed airplanes. But that was kind of a fun time down there with the TBF, and the reason it was is because I worked one week night turn, one week day turn, just like a job. And when you work day turn, you always checked out your airplane about 7:00 o'clock in the morning, and that means you take it off, you fly it out for 40, 50 miles and then come back. And then it's okay for the day and the night, see? And they have a Ready Room, just like all Ready Rooms, and it has a sign above the door just like I think every Ready Room has, and it says, "There are old pilots and there are bold pilots, but there are no old bold pilots." And in this Ready Room they had a huge big map and I would guess offhand -- you got to remember, Tom, this is 56 years ago, and I don't think about that stuff all the time. So my memory's not too keen all the time. So they have this huge map that's maybe 8 feet high and maybe 14 feet long -- of course, that whole area down there -- and they mark very quickly where the problem is. It could be most anything. It could be an airplane down, it could be an airplane with lost engines, and from then on, it's fun. Because what they do is, they close the airport down. The only airplane that's allowed to leave or enter the airport is that TBF, and it's sitting chocked up, and you don't have to adhere to any rules. You get in the airplane and rev it up till it almost shakes apart and you think all the rivets are going to be laying on the ground, and you take off. You can just almost go straight up 'cause you don't have to roll very far. All the red lights are on in the airport. You don't -- you can go between buildings, you can go in places you're not supposed to go, because the main thing is to get that airplane out of there quick. So you have to very quickly look at this big map, get a location, and you have a map board that goes under the instrument panel of a TBF, and I would say it's maybe 18 x 18 inches square; it has big compass rows on it like a computer. It's not electronic, but it's all hand. So you put a location on there and that's your road map, and that's what's gonna to take you out there and bring you back, and that's the scary part. The fun part is that you have all the attention. They have a line with guys going out to the airplane, and I'm so small they literally threw me up into the airplane and put a parachute on me and put a pillow under me 'cause I was only 5'8" and I had to have another cushion to look over the front of the airplane. And you take off and from then on, especially night, it's scary because at, like, 2:00 or 3:00 o'clock in the morning it's pitch black and you may be seventy-five, a hundred miles away from home, and you wonder what you're doing there. And you wonder if you're going to be able to get back. You don't know where you are, only from this map, but you could get disoriented. You start looking around, you forget about the map, and you look for things. For example, I remember one night out about, oh, 3:00 o'clock in the morning, pitch black; the only thing you can see is that white-hot exhaust coming out of the sides of the engine. And the -- an airplane had had an engine quit, and I don't know whether it was shot it down or -- shot down or what it was, or whether the engine was shot at, but I had -- and I think it was a B17 -- so I looked for that thing. I must have looked maybe 10, 15 minutes, and that's when you get lost out there, so you don't know where you are. Sometimes you have a radioman and sometimes you don't, and the radioman orients you sometimes. But this one night, luckily, I found the airplane with blinking lights, and my radioman -- I had a radioman, and he helped me find it. And it was a multi-engine airplane, and one of the engines was feathered, and I understand that another one was about to go. So what I could do -- they didn't land in the water or didn't crash, but what I could do is radio back, tell them my situation and expect them, and I could fly along with them, which I did. I got under one wing and I flew with them -- I don't even know how far it was; I know it was quite a distance -- flew back to Pearl Harbor. When I got there I flapped the wings a little bit and he did, and he landed. I never knew who he was, I never knew anything, but I imagine he felt a little more secure with me there. 'Cause had they gone down like they do sometimes, I could have helped them with life rafts, radios, dye, Very pistols with rockets, and so forth. And we always carried a Gibson Girl radio, and it's not the kind of a girl you think it is {chuckles}. It's little and it's heavy, but it's a radio transmitter, and it's not shaped at all like Marilyn Monroe was shaped. But I mean they're glad to have it when they have it. And you crank it, and it's like a radio. You can send out a signal, and most life rafts had them, see? So we had incidents like that that I could help people, and as I said, no hazardous things where they got shot down and I had to land in the water, which of course I couldn't with a TBF. With a PB2Y I could have. So I spent a lot of time in the water as I -- over the water, and I spent a lot of time in the Ready Room because I was there just like a job, eight, nine hours a day or however. But I got to be real expert at Ping Pong, 'cause that's what I used to do all the time. I didn't -- I read a lot, but you can't read all the time, so I played Ping Pong and ate. So that is mostly my experience with TBF. I got to fly around all the little islands down there. Some I landed on, some I don't even remember the names. I remember French Frigate, I remember Kanton, I remember one island I landed where my hero -- the guy that's on Black Sheep Squadron.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Pappy Boyington?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Pappy Boyington. He was there, and of course they flew -- he was a Marine and they flew Corsairs, and a group of my fellows -- friends down there got to talk to him for awhile. But he was quite interesting, and we didn't know much about him, but we did talk to him and he ended up to be a celebrity.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: You don't remember anything about that conversation though?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: No. After all this time... but if you recall, in the services then in 1943, '44, there were a lot of celebrities in the service, especially a lot of movie stars. And they did -- they showed themselves everywhere for those reason, because they were so... I knew Robert Stack very well at Pearl Harbor. I knew Alan Ladd in Walla Walla; he was a corporal in the Air Force up there and he flew -- or was it -- I think it was in the crew of a B-17. And my instructor in Livermore California, which was like the Steermans that you saw at our air show in Willoughby, he was my instructor. A heck of a nice guy, and that's where I learned acrobatics and all the things you do in a Steerman. And all the girls loved him, as you might imagine, and I asked him a couple of times, "Hey, do you ever see any of your movies?" "No," he said, "I'm in the Navy to fly and I love it, and I don't have time for movies." But a couple of night later they did get him up on stage just to let everybody know that he was there, because then he was quite a celebrity, quite a full-time movie star, if you know what I mean.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Which one are we talking about now?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Robert Taylor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Robert Taylor?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yeah, Robert Taylor. So you did see a lot of those -- those people, and if you talk to old veterans like me they'll tell you, a lot of them, that they saw. And you got to talk to them, and we saw a lot of the female stars and so forth. So that was my best experience and the most fun experience. And a lot our Air-Sea Rescue guys had a lot of problems, had a lot of very hazardous rescues, and I'm sure you've seen movies of a lot of it. And I -- my congratulation goes out to 'em. They're great guys, and I can only say if I had had to do that, and have hazardous duty, I was there to do it. Fortunately for me, I didn't have to. So -- but the other guys that did, I owe a lot of credit to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Were you mostly based in Hawaii, then?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yes, that's the only place I was based. I landed at other islands and so forth, but not, not to stay. I was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Islands around Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yeah, yes. And I was -- what do you call it? -- when I left the Navy... . In our squadron in Kaneohe, we had several airplanes there, Navy airplanes. We had a Corsair there which we were allowed to fly, and we had an F6F we were allowed to fly. I didn't fly that but I did fly the Corsair, mostly just to say that I flew one and to see what it was like; you know you can do it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: So -- but I did have a lot of fun and I'm lucky I got back. And when I did get back I wanted a commercial license, and us pilots back in those days, a lot of the older guys -- which I was not; I was only 21 years old or so -- didn't have all the hours that the old guys had, and they would have like, maybe 10, 15,000. I had only maybe 4,000 hours. But I did want a commercial license and it was very gratifying to know -- like these days it takes a lot of time and money to get a commercial license, and I got mine just in about two minutes, just by signing a form. And I did that, and when I got out I had a good chance to go to United Airlines and a fried of mine -- a friend and myself. And I really chose not to do that because I didn't really want to be away from home that much. And I could have gone there for six weeks to get indoctrinated, and I would have been a multi-engine pilot in -- well, for United Airlines. And one little story I wanted to tell that I always thought was interesting -- you want me to keep going?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: One little story in my training out in California: as you might know, there was always a very friendly rival -- rivalry between the Navy and the Army, and that was back before you had an Air Force. It was all Navy Air Corps and Army Air Corps, and one -- and there were a lot of Navy trainers where the wings fold up. You'd see a lot of 'em flying around out in California because there were a lot of big fields out there. And one day, the P38 Army twin engine -- twin-boom airplane come out, and everybody was raving about this airplane 'cause it was just a grand airplane, the best thing of that date. And as a joke the Air Force pilots -- or Army pilots -- would fly till they'd see a Navy -- one of those little Navy airplanes. And they'd fly up beside you and get your attention. Then they would shut off one engine and feather the props, see, so it didn't go around. Then with the other engine they'd pull away from you like this (demonstrating), see? Ha, ha! Ha! So one day this happened, a P38 came down right beside the Navy plane, only the Navy had a new airplane called a Ryan Fireball. I forget the number of it, but it had a jet in the back -- and not very many people knew this at the time. The Army guy feathered the prop and started to pull away. The Navy guy feathered his only one prop and used the jet and just kind of left them sitting back there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Big joke.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: As a matter of fact, I made a cartoon of that for our museum airplane. So these kind of funny things happened. But I loved the Navy Air Corps, I loved to fly. I don't do much of it any more because I'm 79 years old and I feel better with my feet on the ground, but I get my kicks from the museum. Got a lot of fine people and older veterans like myself and like Bill Willett (ph). Now, he, I imagine, could tell you some very exciting situations because he was a carrier pilot. I was on the Saratoga for almost two weeks but they changed me from there also, so I really never got much carrier experience, but Bill did. So anyway --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: How big was this raft that you would carry, the life raft? How many could it -- how many could it hold? How many men?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, again, I'm only guessing Tom, because this has been years ago, but I would guess it would carry about eight, maybe ten people.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: What altitude could you drop it from?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, we -- we could drop it maybe, oh, 50 feet. Down low, very low.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: And it was -- it would inflate, or they'd inflate it?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yes. And it had paddles and so forth, but they didn't have all the high-tech things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: And I imagine it was pretty choppy in those rough sea waters like that. I remember, speaking of sea waters, when I checked out in PBYs -- if you take that training and you pass it, in other words you get what they call an up check and then they put an arrow on your chalkboard with an arrow pointing up, as an award for winning that and passing that, they gave you a PBY and a crew, and you were allowed to fly to Cuba if you wanted to. And that was very exciting. I had a crew and I flew to Cuba and I was there a couple of nights. But the interesting part was -- and I've had some controversy about this -- in landing a PBY in choppy waters. I had learned, and I have done this, to land perpendicular to the waves. In other words, if you visualize the waves going up, instead of parallel with the low waves you'd land perpendicular. And one of my museum friends showed me an article where that wasn't done or it wasn't so. But I know when I went to Cuba, the Bay, Guantanamo Bay was very, very rough and I remember how I landed. And I was taught to land into the waves, and I did. In fact, the weather was so bad the next day they wouldn't allow me to fly back because I didn't have a green instrument card. You get a pink card and then you get a green card. And they sent a man from Jacksonville that had -- was qualified in instruments to fly me back, and he sat beside me while I flew back. But it was an interesting story, and I'd really like to know the answer to it, whether, let's say, seasoned pilots of PBYs will land parallel to the waves. And if anybody's listening to this is a PBY pilot, you have my phone number, call me and tell me that I'm wrong or right or something. I'd like to know that. I would guess that a PB2Y is the same and I also know that when situations like that happen with very rough, high waves, that we were taught, and I was taught, to do a power stall in a PB2Y, and a power stall is -- you might not know, Tom, but a pilot would -- that it's a very short landing where you land with the power of the engines almost on which slows it down, and it almost literally drops into the water. I'd like to know the answer to that, if everybody does that. So all you PBY pilots, if you're listening -- well, I was going to say turn your tape back but you can't do that. But call Tom --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: That's right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: -- and Tom will give you the... {chuckles}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: What did you do for fun in Cuba when you got there?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: I was there only two nights and I didn't get out. I stayed there and -- till the weather calmed down a little bit and that was it, and went back home. It's only about a hundred miles or something like that, but it was very good experience and I was very proud of the fact that I could do that. And I've loved the PBY, and I think a lot of other people did, 'specially in Air-Sea Rescue. And when I started to fly that, they switched me over to a PB2Y. Mariner, we did not have a PBM Mariner; I've never flown one of those. So that's kind of my story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Were there some buddies or anything, close friends that you had there in the service over there?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: No; you'd think you would know your buddies and keep in touch, and a couple of 'em I called, and I don't think I ever could get 'em, and the time goes fast. I did have one buddy, my best buddy in -- lived in Chicago, and he and I went through most of our training together. And in other words, when I soloed the TBF he watched me, and when he soloed I watched him. I did keep in track -- in touch with him in Chicago. He worked for Meyer that makes the hot dogs. And his son got to be an airline pilot, and his name was Nels Olaf Ingren (ph), a Swede. And we were like two buddies, and they called us Inky and Dinky because of my name "Dig" and his name "Ingren," so they called us Inky and Dinky. But everyplace one of us was, the other went. We got our wings together, and he's about the only one that I've stayed close to at all, but he passed away, I'd say about four years ago. And I knew his wife and I'd get in touch with her, and when I'd be in Chicago on business I'd stop in to see both of them, and then that kind of died out and he -- he passed away. So I'm lucky I'm still going, Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Did you have many USO shows that you saw when you were over there in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, no. I had a good friend that was kind of a celebrity in the USO; he sang with the orchestras. I used to sing before -- well, I sang in a Barbershop Quartet and he was in our quartet and he was very, very good. But I do remember one incident that you might find interesting. In Pearl Harbor, I was there on D-Day, and in Hawaii there was a radio station that {clearing throat} that we listened to the music every evening, the current music, whatever it was. And there was a man that owned a very -- he was a celebrity, a very rich man in Honolulu, and I'm trying to think of his name; maybe it'll come to me. He had this huge big name -- a huge big restaurant, and he always said in his advertisement -- after he talked about the veterans because he loved them -- and he says, "The day the war ends, my restaurant is open to veterans, all of them." I'm trying to think of his name while I'm talking with you; it's not coming to me. And you know that he did this. We couldn't believe that he did this, and it must have cost most of his fortune --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: -- when he did, but he did open it to everybody: officers, enlisted men, any part of it, and you could go in there during that day, get all the drinks you want, do anything you want, and as I remember, I couldn't get into the place, or me and my friends would have gotten in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: On VE Day?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: It was on D-Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: On D-Day, oh.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: And that's the reason he did it, because he said on that day he was gonna do this. And we didn't think he'd do it; he kept saying in his advertisements, it would say he'd do this, but he did it, and he did do it. It cost a lot of bucks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Letters from home, do you remember anything about that?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, I wasn't married at the time, and I did get a lot of letters from the girl I intended marry, and I did marry the one that I intended to marry, the one I took to the high school prom; I married her. But I had a very good experience in the Navy and I'm very proud of the Navy and I always have been.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: When you think about that, does anything come to mind as your most vivid memory of that time overseas?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, it would be in -- at the times the Air-Sea Rescue was taking place and the excitement of getting to them and finding them and getting lost, and I was just about as scared as anybody else at 3:00 or 4:00 o'clock in the morning and not know what I -- where I am and what the heck I'm doin' there in the first place. It shakes you up a little, but you're trained to know what to do. And fortunately, you have the presence of mind to do it and get back home, but it isn't easy sometimes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Did you learn to like the TBF?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, not really. Not really. It's a big airplane; I couldn't see over the nose of it because I was so short, and I had to have pillows under me, but I did it, and we had that -- along with the other airplanes at the airport where we were, the airfield -- we had also a couple of Piper Cubs, and you know what a Piper Cub is. Well, we had to get so many hours on that each month, and none of us wanted to fly it. It was like getting into a kite, you know, or something like this, and finally they said, "You're going to fly it whether you want to or not," and they'd put our names on the board, a day and a time, and we would have to go and fly it, maybe two or three hours or something, just to put hours on it. And I remember after flying that TBF and all those multi-engine planes, I had a heck of a time getting it down on the ground. You come in to land and {laughs} it wanted to just stay up in the air like a kite. But it was fun and you got a lot of experience doing all that, so I had a lot of fun with it, a lot of fun playing Ping Pong. And then fortunately for me, after I got out of the service I took advantage of the GI Bill, which a lot of veterans did not, which was a mistake. So I took a -- I went to Carnegie Mellon in Pittsburg, because I lived in East Liverpool. Fortunately, I started at the right time of the year where the semesters ended and started, and I went through that in three years and I got my degree, and I have a degree in Industrial Design which is a profession right in the middle between being an artist and a designer. And most people don't know what that is, but it's very well known. So that's part of my Navy experience and what I got of being out of it. As I say, I loved it; still do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Of all the planes that you did get a chance to fly, what did you like the best?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Well, I'd say I flew the twin-engine Beechcraft. It's a smaller airplane and it was pretty much like the A20 only it was, of course, a lot smaller. And I enjoyed that. We'd go out, we did our night navigation, and in the Navy at the time, the pilots did not have navigators like the Army. We had to do this ourselves. Now, I remember I told you we were rivals; we did this ourselves. And then the PBY and the PB2Y, we had a big desk and we would take turns navigating. While the Army pilots slept or napped, we would have to go and navigate to find where we were, if you see what I mean. But we loved them, Tom. {Coughs} Excuse me. But I did enjoy the Beechcraft. As a matter of fact, after I -- is this stuff important enough to tell you about?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: I just -- I'm interested now {laughs}. I just want to hear it.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Before I got my wings, a week before I got my wings, we had to pass a test in navigation -- I just mentioned navigation -- and you had to pass them all or you didn't get your wings. My friend from Chicago, Nels, passed his, and in that last week when I took my night navigation, I had to get three 3-star locations; that's the way you find yourself with an octant compass. I got only one; it's one of those nights. Well, they wouldn't give me my wings, but what they did do, they'd say, "We're going to give you a week, and if in one week you can come back and do the same thing, you'll get your wings." 'Cause they were giving you wings like a week apart down there. As a matter of fact, President Bush got his wings down there, and he flew a TBF too. And he had a lot of hazardous duty that I hadn't -- didn't have, and that's the reason I'm kind of embarrassed to talk about the rescue and all that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: It's all part of the story.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yeah. So anyway, my friend Nels waited for me for a week until I learned the stars well enough that I got three 3-star fixes. Well, you can believe I spent a lot of nights on my back in the evening. It's nice in Texas, and after a week I was ready to take this again, and I did; I got three 3-star fixes. And this was the Beechcraft. So I got my wings and my friend waited; he got his wings and we stood side-by-side, got our wings pinned on and threw our hats up in the air, and we went from there on together, went to Hawaii -- and I think that's important... but he's passed away now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Getting back to before the -- before you went in, do you have any memories of when they attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Yes, and I'm trying to think of where I was. I know better where I was when they dropped the atomic bomb. I was in -- I had a girlfriend in San Diego, and I had been living at a hotel in Coronado, Coronado Bay. And I was at dinner at her house with her folks, and I heard on the radio that they had dropped the atomic bomb. And for Pearl Harbor, you know that I can't remember where I was? I could maybe trace back some way at the year. I'd have to know -- I don't even remember the year it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: 1941, so you were what, about 19, maybe? Or something like that?

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: That sounds about right. Maybe I wasn't interested in airplanes then, you know, to do what I did. But when the crisis came, I did go out and enlist, and I've never been sorry for it. One other thing about the TBF with pilots or men that have flown them; when I checked out in this, one of the things they had you do was to go round and round the airport and land several times to get that experience before you were checked out. Well, if you know the flaps on an airplane go down when you're landing and when you're taking off, the flaps on that TBF was on a lever like you might have on your lawnmower. And when you come in to land you push the lever down, the flaps would go down, and then you would pull it up halfway and they would lock. Well, my buddy's down here watching me land, and I don't know how many times I did that, but the last one I come in, I remember the girl in the tower said, "Mr. Digman, which one of those was your final landing?" 'cause it bounced, see. So I come in and I met my friend Nels, and I said, "Boy, you better watch that thing, 'cause it lands hot." like maybe a hundred, over a hundred miles an hour. He says, "No wonder you were pulling the flaps up." And here what I had done, I put the flaps down; I pulled them up halfway to lock them, and I was pulling them all the way up. So I landed that airplane a lot of times without flaps. And when some pilot hears that, they'll wonder how I did it, and I do to; I wonder. That was exciting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Yeah {chuckling}.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: Boy, was it exciting. So anyway --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: I'm with you there.

sp.speaker: Bernard Digman
sp.p: A: All the other things, Tom, I don't know whether -- I'd have to think and write some more.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: All right, that's fine.
